title: What is the Small Claims Tribunal?
summary: A quick, plain-language introduction to what the SCT does and what kinds of disputes it typically handles.
content: The Small Claims Tribunal (SCT) is a forum designed to let people resolve certain civil disputes without needing a lawyer.
It generally handles disputes such as claims over goods and services, and some tenancy-related claims, within a set claim-value limit.
Proceedings are meant to be simpler and faster than a full court case, and are generally conducted by the parties themselves.

Always verify current jurisdiction, limits, and procedure on the official State Courts / Community Justice and Tribunals System resources - this lesson is a general orientation, not a procedural guide.

check.question: Who typically represents the parties in an SCT hearing?
options: Always a lawyer
The parties themselves, generally without lawyers
A police officer
A jury
check.explanation: SCT proceedings are designed to be accessible without a lawyer, though rules on when representation is allowed can vary - verify current rules if unsure.

title: Why evidence matters more than memory
summary: Understand why documents, messages, and photos usually matter more than your recollection of events.
content: Memory fades and can be challenged. Written records - receipts, messages, contracts, photos - are generally harder to dispute.
A useful habit: whenever a dispute starts, write down a dated timeline of what happened while it's fresh, and gather any documents immediately.
If an agreement was only verbal, look for indirect evidence: payment records, messages referencing the agreement, or witnesses.
This does not mean a claim without perfect evidence is hopeless - it means identifying gaps early lets you decide what more to gather.

check.question: If an agreement was only made verbally, what can still help support your case?
options: Nothing can help
Payment records or messages referencing the agreement
Only a written contract counts
Waiting until the hearing to explain it well
check.explanation: Indirect evidence like payment records, messages, or witnesses can meaningfully support an otherwise verbal agreement.

title: Time limits: why waiting can cost you your claim
summary: A short explainer on why claims generally can't be brought indefinitely, and why checking time limits early matters.
content: Most civil claims are subject to a 'limitation period' - a deadline, counted from when the issue arose, after which you may lose the right to sue.
Limitation periods vary by claim type and jurisdiction, and this app does not calculate them for you.
The practical lesson: don't sit on a dispute. Check the applicable time limit early, ideally with an official or professional source.
Delay can also weaken a case even where a claim is still technically in time, since evidence and memory degrade.

check.question: What is a 'limitation period'?
options: The maximum amount you can claim
A deadline for bringing a claim after which the right to sue may be lost
The length of a tribunal hearing
A limit on how many witnesses you can call
check.explanation: A limitation period is a time limit for bringing a claim - not a claim-value cap or hearing length.

title: Understanding the other side's likely arguments
summary: Why anticipating counterarguments - rather than only building your own story - is one of the strongest things you can do to prepare.
content: A one-sided account, however true, is rarely the full picture a tribunal will hear. The other side will have their own version.
Strong preparation means asking: what will they say happened instead? What will they say I'm missing or got wrong?
This is exactly what this app's Opposing Party and Tribunal Questioning modes are for - practising against pushback before it happens for real.
Being able to calmly respond to a counterargument with evidence is often more persuasive than a passionate but unchallenged narrative.

check.question: What is the main benefit of anticipating the other side's arguments before a hearing?
options: It guarantees you will win
It lets you prepare calm, evidence-based responses instead of being caught off guard
It is not useful, only your own story matters
It replaces the need for evidence
check.explanation: Anticipating counterarguments helps you prepare responses and identify evidence gaps - it doesn't guarantee an outcome.

title: Deposits: what 'fair wear and tear' usually means
summary: A short explainer on the common deposit-dispute distinction between damage and normal wear and tear.
content: Landlords can generally deduct from a deposit for damage caused by the tenant, but not for 'fair wear and tear' - the ordinary, gradual deterioration that happens through normal use.
Photos taken at move-in and move-out are one of the strongest ways to settle disagreements about condition.
If deductions seem excessive, ask for an itemised breakdown and, where possible, receipts or quotes for the claimed repairs.
This is general guidance - the specific tenancy agreement's terms govern the actual dispute.

check.question: What is generally NOT deductible from a security deposit?
options: Unpaid rent
Damage caused by the tenant
Fair wear and tear from normal use
Unpaid utility bills
check.explanation: Fair wear and tear is the ordinary deterioration from normal use, which is generally distinguished from tenant-caused damage.

title: Lending money informally: reducing 'he said, she said'
summary: Practical habits that make informal loans between individuals much easier to prove later.
content: Informal loans between friends or family are common, and also commonly disputed, because terms are rarely written down.
Even a short text message confirming 'this is a loan of $X, to be repaid by [date]' can be far more useful later than a verbal promise.
Bank transfer records establish that money moved, but not necessarily that it was a loan rather than a gift - the surrounding messages matter.
If you're currently owed money informally, consider (respectfully) getting the other party to confirm the terms in writing now, before a dispute escalates.

check.question: Why might a bank transfer record alone not be enough to prove a loan?
options: Banks don't keep records
It shows money moved but not that both parties agreed it was a loan rather than a gift
Transfers are not admissible evidence
It is always enough on its own
check.explanation: A transfer shows money moved, but surrounding context (messages, agreement) is usually needed to show it was a loan, not a gift.
